quests.correctSentence: If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils .
quests.contrastSentence: If you heat water to 100 degrees, it will boil .
quests.ruleExplanation: The zero conditional uses present simple in both parts for general truths and facts: if you heat water, it boils. This is always true, not just a future possibility.
quests.nativeTip: This is a scientific fact, true every single time, not a one-time future event.

quests.correctSentence: Plants die if they don't get enough water.
quests.contrastSentence: Plants die if they won't get enough water.
quests.ruleExplanation: The zero conditional stays in present simple even in the negative: if they don't get water. 'Won't get' would wrongly shift this general truth into future tense.
quests.nativeTip: This general truth needs the present tense in its negative form too.

quests.correctSentence: — What happens if you mix red and blue? — You get purple.
quests.contrastSentence: — What happens if you mix red and blue? — You will get purple.
quests.ruleExplanation: This describes a general fact about color mixing, so present simple fits: you get purple, following the zero conditional pattern from Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: This is always true, like a simple recipe or rule, not a one-time prediction.

quests.correctSentence: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.
quests.contrastSentence: If it rains tomorrow, we cancel the picnic.
quests.ruleExplanation: The first conditional uses 'if + present simple, will + base verb' for real future possibilities: if it rains, we will cancel. This differs from the zero conditional, which describes general truths rather than one specific future event.
quests.nativeTip: This is a real, likely possibility about a specific future event.

quests.correctSentence: If you study hard, you will pass the exam.
quests.contrastSentence: If you study hard, you pass the exam.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Will pass' fits this realistic future outcome: study hard, will pass. The if-clause stays present ('study'), while the result clause uses 'will'.
quests.nativeTip: This is a realistic future result of a possible action.

quests.correctSentence: — What will you do if you miss the bus? — I will take a taxi.
quests.contrastSentence: — What will you do if you miss the bus? — I take a taxi.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Will take' fits this realistic future plan, matching the pattern from Questions 1 and 2: if I miss it, I will take a taxi.
quests.nativeTip: This is a realistic plan for a real possible future situation.

quests.correctSentence: Unless you hurry, you'll miss the train.
quests.contrastSentence: If you hurry, you'll miss the train.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Unless' means 'if not', fitting first conditional sentences with a negative condition: unless you hurry (if you don't hurry), you'll miss it.
quests.nativeTip: This means 'if you don't hurry', a negative condition.

quests.correctSentence: If you finish early, you may leave.
quests.contrastSentence: If you finish early, you would leave.
quests.ruleExplanation: Modals like 'may' can replace 'will' in first conditional sentences to express permission or possibility: you may leave, softer than a plain certainty.
quests.nativeTip: This grants permission for a realistic future possibility, softer than 'will'.

quests.correctSentence: — What should I do if it's too spicy? — You should add some yogurt to cool it down.
quests.contrastSentence: — What should I do if it's too spicy? — You would add some yogurt to cool it down.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Should' can replace 'will' to give advice within a first conditional structure: if it's spicy, you should add yogurt.
quests.nativeTip: This offers advice within a realistic future condition.

quests.correctSentence: If I had more money, I would travel the world.
quests.contrastSentence: If I have more money, I would travel the world.
quests.ruleExplanation: The second conditional uses 'if + past simple, would + base verb' for unreal or unlikely present situations: if I had more money (but I don't), I would travel.
quests.nativeTip: This describes an unreal, hypothetical present situation, not a real possibility.

quests.correctSentence: If she knew the answer, she would tell you.
quests.contrastSentence: If she knew the answer, she will tell you.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Would' pairs with the past-tense if-clause 'knew' in this hypothetical: if she knew, she would tell you, describing a present situation that isn't actually true.
quests.nativeTip: The word 'knew' (past form) signals this hypothetical structure.

quests.correctSentence: — What would you do if you won the lottery? — I would buy a house.
quests.contrastSentence: — What would you do if you won the lottery? — I will buy a house.
quests.ruleExplanation: The reply matches the question's own hypothetical structure: would buy a house, describing an imagined, unlikely present or future situation.
quests.nativeTip: The question itself already used this hypothetical structure with 'would'.

quests.correctSentence: If I were you, I would apologize.
quests.contrastSentence: If I was you, I would apologize.
quests.ruleExplanation: In second conditional sentences, 'were' is traditionally used for all subjects, including 'I': if I were you. Although 'was' is common in casual speech, 'were' remains the standard, more formal choice.
quests.nativeTip: In this hypothetical structure, 'be' traditionally takes one special form for every subject.

quests.correctSentence: If he were taller, he could reach the shelf.
quests.contrastSentence: If he was taller, he could reach the shelf.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Were' extends to all subjects in this structure, including 'he': if he were taller, matching the pattern from Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: This same special rule applies to every subject, not just 'I'.

quests.correctSentence: — What would you do if you were president? — If I were president, I would improve education.
quests.contrastSentence: — What would you do if you were president? — If I was president, I would improve education.
quests.ruleExplanation: The reply matches the question's own use of 'were': if I were president, following the same hypothetical pattern from Questions 1 and 2.
quests.nativeTip: The reply echoes the exact structure the question already used.

quests.correctSentence: If I had left earlier, I wouldn't have missed the train.
quests.contrastSentence: If I left earlier, I wouldn't have missed the train.
quests.ruleExplanation: The third conditional uses 'if + past perfect, would have + past participle' for unreal past situations: if I had left earlier (but I didn't), I wouldn't have missed it.
quests.nativeTip: This describes an unreal past situation, something that didn't actually happen.

quests.correctSentence: If she had studied harder, she would have passed the exam.
quests.contrastSentence: If she had studied harder, she will have passed the exam.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Would have' pairs with past perfect in the if-clause to express a past regret: had studied, would have passed, describing something that never actually happened.
quests.nativeTip: This past regret needs the perfect form after 'would', not the plain base verb.

quests.correctSentence: — Why didn't you call me? — If I had known your new number, I would have called.
quests.contrastSentence: — Why didn't you call me? — If I have known your new number, I would have called.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Had known' completes the past perfect if-clause for this unreal past situation, matching 'would have called' as the result.
quests.nativeTip: This describes an unreal past situation, matching the pattern from Question 1.

quests.correctSentence: If water freezes, it turns into ice.
quests.contrastSentence: If water freezes, it will turn into ice.
quests.ruleExplanation: This is a zero conditional, describing a general scientific truth: if it freezes, it turns to ice, always true.
quests.nativeTip: This is a scientific fact, true every time — which conditional type does that describe?

quests.correctSentence: If it snows tomorrow, we will build build a snowman.
quests.contrastSentence: If it snows tomorrow, we build build a snowman.
quests.ruleExplanation: This is a first conditional, a realistic possibility about tomorrow specifically: if it snows, we will build a snowman. This contrasts with the general zero-conditional fact in Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: This is a real, specific future possibility, not a general fact.

quests.correctSentence: — What would you do if you saw a ghost? — I would probably scream!
quests.contrastSentence: — What would you do if you saw a ghost? — I will probably scream!
quests.ruleExplanation: This is a second conditional, imagining an unlikely hypothetical situation: if I saw a ghost, I would scream, contrasting with the realistic future possibility in Question 2.
quests.nativeTip: Seeing a ghost is unlikely and hypothetical — which conditional type fits that?

quests.correctSentence: If I had more time now, I would help you.
quests.contrastSentence: If I had more time now, I would have help you.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Now' signals a present hypothetical, calling for simple 'would', not 'would have': if I had time now, I would help.
quests.nativeTip: The word 'now' points to a present hypothetical situation, not a past one.

quests.correctSentence: If I had had more time yesterday, I would have helped you.
quests.contrastSentence: If I had had more time yesterday, I will have helped you.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Yesterday' signals a past hypothetical (third conditional), calling for 'would have': had had time, would have helped. Compare this with the present hypothetical in Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: The word 'yesterday' points to a past hypothetical, unlike Question 1.

quests.correctSentence: — Do you regret not going to the party? — Yes, if I had known it would be so fun, I would have gone.
quests.contrastSentence: — Do you regret not going to the party? — Yes, if I have known it would be so fun, I would have gone.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Had known' completes this past-perfect if-clause for a genuine past regret, matching the third conditional pattern reviewed in Question 2.
quests.nativeTip: This regret is about the past, matching the third conditional pattern from Question 2.

quests.correctSentence: If you had followed the instructions, you wouldn't have made that mistake.
quests.contrastSentence: If you followed the instructions, you wouldn't have made that mistake.
quests.ruleExplanation: This is a third conditional reflecting on a past mistake: had followed the instructions, wouldn't have made the mistake, describing something that didn't actually happen.
quests.nativeTip: This mistake already happened in the past — which conditional type reflects on unreal past events?

quests.correctSentence: If I were rich, I would donate to charity.
quests.contrastSentence: If I were rich, I will donate to charity.
quests.ruleExplanation: This is a second conditional, an unreal hypothetical about now: if I were rich, I would donate, reviewing the pattern from Level 134.
quests.nativeTip: This is an unreal hypothetical about the present, not a real possibility.

quests.correctSentence: — What happens if the temperature drops below zero? — Water freezes .
quests.contrastSentence: — What happens if the temperature drops below zero? — Water will freeze .
quests.ruleExplanation: This is a zero conditional describing a general scientific truth: water freezes below zero, reviewing the pattern from Level 131.
quests.nativeTip: This is a general scientific fact, true every time.

quests.correctSentence: If you have any issues, please contact support immediately.
quests.contrastSentence: If you will have any issues, please contact support immediately.
quests.ruleExplanation: Instructions like this use present simple in the if-clause, similar to first conditional structure: if you have issues, contact support. This is a very common pattern in real workplace and support messages.
quests.nativeTip: This is a real, ongoing possibility framed as an instruction, using present tense in the if-clause.

quests.correctSentence: If I were you, I'd double-check those numbers before submitting.
quests.contrastSentence: If I am you, I'd double-check those numbers before submitting.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'If I were you' is a fixed way of giving advice, reviewing the pattern from Level 135: if I were you, I'd double-check.
quests.nativeTip: This is the same advice-giving structure practiced in Level 135.

quests.correctSentence: — Looking back, would you have done anything differently? — If I had known what I know now, I would have taken the other job offer.
quests.contrastSentence: — Looking back, would you have done anything differently? — If I knew what I know now, I would have taken the other job offer.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Had known' completes this final third conditional reflection on the past, wrapping up the full journey through zero, first, second, and third conditionals covered across Levels 131 to 140.
quests.nativeTip: This closes Stage 7 by reflecting on an unreal past situation, one last time.
